title: Learning when the signal is weak
objectives: Explain why prediction in finance differs: low signal to noise, changing regimes and leakage.

screens.title: A small correlation
screens.prose: About two and a half minutes a question, longer for the code; say your reasoning aloud first. A signal correlates 0.05 with next-day returns. Its $t$ statistic over $n$ days is $r\sqrt{n - 2}/\sqrt{1 - r^2}$, drawn as the curve. Drag the point along it.
screens.question: Over 250 days, what is $t$?

hints.text: Drag the point to $n = 250$ and read its label.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the curve at 250 days.

byKey.r: That is the correlation. Multiply by $\sqrt{n - 2}$.
byKey.z: That is the 5% line the curve has not reached yet.
byKey.p: That is the p-value. The question asks for $t$.

explain.text: A year of data gives $t = 0.79$, far below 1.96. A real signal this small looks like noise for years.

screens.title: How long to wait
screens.prose: Same signal, same curve. Drag to see where it crosses 1.96.
screens.question: Fill in the table.

hints.text: Read the curve at 500 and 1,000.
$t$ grows like $\sqrt{n}$: doubling the days multiplies it by about 1.41.
1.1172, 1.5815, and the crossing at 1,535 days.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the curve, then find where it meets 1.96.

explain.text: $t$ grows with the square root of the days. It reaches 1.96 at 1,535 days, about six years of daily data.

screens.title: The days needed
screens.prose: Derive the days needed for $|t| \ge 1.96$ at correlation $r$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.why: You squared the right side but not the 1.96. That gives about 785 days, half enough.

hints.text: Start from the condition on $t$.
Isolate $\sqrt{n - 2}$, then square both sides.
Every factor on the right gets squared, 1.96 included.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Condition, isolate, square, substitute.

byKey.x: You left 1.96 unsquared. The bound is $1.96^2 \approx 3.84$ times $(1 - r^2)/r^2$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: Roughly $n \approx (1.96/r)^2$: at $r = 0.05$ that is 1,537, close to the exact 1,535. Halving $r$ quadruples the days.

screens.title: What 0.05 is worth
screens.prose: Hold a position equal to the signal's z-score $s$ each day. Returns are $r = 0.05s + \sqrt{1 - 0.05^2}\,e$. Daily P&L $sr$ has mean 0.05 and variance $1 + 0.05^2$.

state.caption: 300 seeded days with a true correlation of 0.05.

screens.question: What is the annual Sharpe ratio, over 252 days?

hints.text: Daily Sharpe is mean over standard deviation.
Multiply by $\sqrt{252} = 15.87$.

feedback.correct: $0.04994 \times 15.87 = 0.7927$. A seeded run of 4 million days gives 0.78, within its noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by the standard deviation, then scale by $\sqrt{252}$.

byKey.daily: That is the daily Sharpe ratio. Annualise with $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.naive: You used $0.05\sqrt{252}$ and dropped the $\sqrt{1 + 0.05^2}$. Close, but not the value.

explain.text: A correlation of 0.05, traded every day, gives an annual Sharpe ratio near 0.79. The cloud looks round, yet the P&L is worth having.

screens.title: Too small to matter?
screens.prose: A candidate looks at the cloud and says: "A correlation of 0.05 is too small to matter."

state.caption: 300 seeded days with a true correlation of 0.05.

screens.question: What do you say?

options.text: If it is real it matters: traded daily, it is worth a Sharpe ratio near 0.8.
Agreed: only correlations above 0.3 are useful, and 0.05 is far below that.
options.why: You judged by the picture. In finance a real 0.05 traded daily is a good signal.

options.text: Its $R^2$ is 0.0025, so it explains too little of each day's return to use.
options.why: Small $R^2$ per day is normal for returns. What counts is the edge over many bets.

options.text: It matters only if $t > 1.96$ within a year of daily data, about 250 days.
options.why: A year gives $t = 0.79$ for a real 0.05. Significance needs about six years.

hints.text: Recall the Sharpe ratio you just found.
Edge per bet is small; the number of bets is large.
A real 0.05 daily gives about 0.79 a year.

feedback.correct: Small per bet, large over many bets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh the edge per day against the number of days.

byKey.agree: That is the trap. Return correlations of a few per cent are what good signals look like.

explain.text: Returns are mostly noise, so useful signals correlate a few per cent. Breadth turns a small edge into a good Sharpe ratio, if the edge is real.

screens.title: The best of fifty
screens.prose: You test 50 features of pure noise against 250 days of returns and keep the best. Each sample correlation is roughly normal with sd $1/\sqrt{250}$. The expected largest of 50 absolute standard normals is 2.5096.

state.caption: Run the experiment. Each trial is 50 noise features on 250 days.

screens.question: What is the expected best $|r|$?

hints.text: Scale the 2.5096 to correlation units.
One correlation has sd $1/\sqrt{250} = 0.0632$.

byKey.one: That is the sd of one noise correlation. The best of 50 is about 2.5 sd.
byKey.mean: That is the average $|r|$ of one feature, not the best of 50.

explain.text: The best of 50 noise features shows $|r| \approx 0.16$, three times the real signal above. In sample it looks strong; out of sample it has nothing. The histogram centres near 0.1587.

screens.title: A feature that knows today
screens.prose: Returns are independent with equal variance. A feature on day $t$ is the mean of $r_t$, $r_{t-1}$ and $r_{t-2}$. It is used to predict $r_t$.

state.caption: The feature on day $t$ averages $r_{t-2}$, $r_{t-1}$ and $r_t$.

screens.question: What is the correlation between the feature and $r_t$?

hints.text: Find the covariance and the two variances.
The covariance is $\sigma^2/3$ and the feature's variance is $\sigma^2/3$.
$(\sigma^2/3)/(\sigma \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{3}) = 1/\sqrt{3}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Covariance over the product of the standard deviations.

byKey.rsq: That is $R^2$, the square of the correlation.
byKey.zero: That is the honest, lagged feature. This one includes today.
byKey.one: Only a third of the feature is today, so the link is partial.

explain.text: The window holds today's return, so the feature "predicts" it with correlation 0.5774 and $R^2 = 1/3$. Shift it by one day and the correlation is 0.

screens.title: After costs
screens.prose: A daily rule expects to gain 5 basis points a day. It replaces its whole position every day: it sells yesterday's and buys today's. Each trade costs 3 basis points.
screens.question: What is its expected net gain per day, in basis points?

hints.text: Count the trades each day.
Two trades a day at 3 bp each.

byKey.oneside: You charged one trade. Replacing a position is a sale and a purchase.
byKey.sign: Selling yesterday's position and buying today's is two trades, 6 bp, so 5 − 6 is below zero. A positive 1 takes 6 − 5, the wrong way round.

explain.text: A small edge traded often is eaten by costs. Trading less often, or only on strong signals, keeps more of it.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose:
What you used:
$$t = \frac{r\sqrt{n - 2}}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}}, \qquad n \approx \left(\frac{1.96}{r}\right)^2$$
Said aloud: "Returns are mostly noise, so a good signal correlates a few per cent. Proving one takes years, and the best of many noise features looks as good. So I test out of sample in time order, check for leakage and costs."
screens.question: Which answer would you give an interviewer?

options.text: "Signals are weak: I judge them by $t$, sample size and a time-ordered test, then check leakage and costs."
"I keep the features with a high $R^2$ in sample, since that shows they already explain the returns."
options.why: In-sample $R^2$ rewards the best of many noise features and leaked ones.

options.text: "I use shuffled cross-validation to be safe, so that every fold sees a fair mix of all the regimes."
options.why: Shuffling mixes future and past days, which leaks (`validation` l5-shuffling-lies).

options.text: "A deep network will find the signal, since it can fit patterns a linear model misses."
options.why: More flexibility fits more noise when the signal is this weak.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the answer that names the tests.

explain.text: A strong answer says why finance differs: low signal to noise. It then names the checks: $t$, sample size, time-ordered tests, leakage and costs.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "It is significant in sample. Do you trade it?"
screens.question: Which answer would you give?

options.text: "Not yet: I test it walk-forward on later data, after costs and in each sub-period, then trade small."
"Yes: $t = 3.93$ is far above 1.96, so the chance that this is pure luck is well under 1%."
options.why: In-sample $t$ ignores how many lags you tried, regime change and costs.

options.text: "No: a correlation of 0.12 is too small to trade, since it explains under 2% of each day's move."
options.why: A real 0.12 would be a strong daily signal; the question is whether it is real.

options.text: "Yes, with leverage: it is significant, and a signal this strong deserves a large position from day one."
options.why: Size follows evidence out of sample, not in-sample $t$.

hints.text: In sample is where you found it.
Out-of-sample tests in time order, and costs, decide.
A coefficient can be +0.1 in one regime and −0.1 in the next.

feedback.correct: Find in sample, prove out of sample, then size small.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the answer that tests before trading.

explain.text: Fitting in sample is the start. A walk-forward test, costs and stability across sub-periods decide; `research-int` l13-baseline-first takes this further.

ideas: A real return signal correlates a few per cent; $t = r\sqrt{n - 2}/\sqrt{1 - r^2}$ needs years to reach 1.96.
Small edges add up over many bets, but costs and the best-of-many effect can wipe them out.
A feature whose window includes the target leaks: the mean of three returns "predicts" today with $r = 1/\sqrt{3}$.
summary.trap: A correlation of 0.05 is not too small to matter: traded daily, it gives a Sharpe ratio near 0.8.
